topic: IAS 1 – order of balance sheet items
prompt: Meridian presents (in this order) non-current assets, current assets, current liabilities and non-current liabilities. Is this order of presentation mandatory under IFRS? Explain.
modelAnswer: No. IAS 1 lists the line items that must at least be presented and requires a current/non-current distinction (unless a liquidity presentation is more relevant), but it does not prescribe a format or order. Companies may present non-current items first (common in the UK and continental Europe) or current items first, and may present a “net assets” format as Meridian does.
keyPoints: IAS 1 prescribes minimum line items, not format or order

steps.title: Recall IAS 1
steps.why: IAS 1 requires minimum line items and a current/non-current distinction (unless a liquidity presentation is more relevant) – but NO format or order.

steps.title: Apply
steps.why: Non-current first and a 'net assets' format is common in the UK; others present current items first or equity before liabilities.

prompt: Meridian shows liabilities in brackets as negative numbers to calculate “net assets”. Why? What is the meaning of net assets?
modelAnswer: Net assets = total assets − total liabilities = equity (here 54,260 − 18,700 − 31,160 = 4,400). Deducting the liabilities leads directly to the book (accounting) value of the group that belongs to the shareholders; because net assets equal equity, the bottom part of the balance sheet then shows how this equity is composed (share capital, premium, reserves, NCI).

steps.title: Meaning
steps.why: Deducting liabilities leads straight to the book value belonging to the shareholders; the composition of that equity follows below.
steps.result: Net assets = equity = book value (not market value)

prompt: Explain what the non-controlling interests (NCI) in equity represent and comment on the amount of NCI in Meridian's balance sheet.
modelAnswer: NCI is the part of the equity of consolidated subsidiaries that does not belong to the parent but to other (minority) shareholders of those subsidiaries; under full consolidation 100% of the subsidiaries' assets and liabilities are included, so their share of net assets is shown separately within equity. Comment: Meridian's NCI (3,300) is three times the equity of the parent's shareholders (1,100) – most of the group's equity is provided by minority shareholders of subsidiaries (e.g. a large, partly owned subsidiary). The parent's own equity is small because retained earnings are negative (5,400) – e.g. after buybacks, dividends or losses.
keyPoints: Share of subsidiaries' equity held by other shareholders
Large partly owned subsidiaries / negative retained earnings

steps.title: Define NCI
steps.why: Full consolidation includes 100% of each subsidiary; the part of their net assets owned by other shareholders is shown separately within equity as NCI.

steps.title: Read Meridian's figures
lines: NCI 3,300 vs shareholders' equity 1,100 → NCI = 3 × parent equity
Retained earnings −5,400 → parent equity small (buy-backs, dividends or losses)

steps.title: Comment
steps.why: A large share of the group's equity comes from minority shareholders of partly owned subsidiaries.
steps.result: Most group equity is NCI – large partly owned subsidiaries

prompt: What is the meaning of the line “Adjustments reconciling profit after tax to operating cash flows”? Give one example of such an adjustment.
modelAnswer: Meridian uses the indirect method: it starts from profit after tax and adjusts it for items that affected profit but not cash. Non-cash expenses are added back (depreciation, amortisation, impairment, increase in provisions), non-cash income is deducted, and changes in working capital are reflected (an increase in receivables or inventories reduces cash; an increase in payables increases it). Example: depreciation of 1,000 lowers profit but not cash, so it is added back.

steps.title: Identify the method
steps.why: Starting from profit after tax → indirect method.

steps.title: What the adjustments contain
lines: + non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortisation, impairment, increase in provisions)
− non-cash income (e.g. gains on disposal, share of profit of associates)
± working-capital changes (↑ receivables/inventory = cash ↓; ↑ payables = cash ↑)

steps.title: Example
lines: Depreciation 1,000: reduced profit but no cash outflow → added back
steps.result: Adjustments turn accounting profit into operating cash

prompt: Meridian's cash flow from investing activities is negative. Explain briefly whether this is good or bad news.
modelAnswer: A negative investing cash flow is normal and generally good news: the company invests to maintain or expand its capacity (PPE, intangibles such as R&D and licences, acquisitions), which shows that management sees opportunities. Here the investments (2,700) are fully covered by operating cash flow (4,400), so they are self-financed. A final judgement requires knowing what was bought (which activities, countries, acquisitions) and whether these investments will earn more than their cost of capital.
keyPoints: Depends on type and quality of investments

steps.title: Read the sign
steps.why: Negative investing cash flow = net investment in PPE, intangibles (R&D, licences) or acquisitions.

steps.title: Check financing capacity
lines: Operating cash flow 4,400 > investing outflow 2,700 → self-financed

steps.title: Judge
steps.why: Normally good news (capacity maintained/expanded), but what was bought and whether it earns more than its cost of capital must still be checked.

prompt: Prepare the consolidated balance sheet of the PC group at the acquisition date. Explain your calculations, in particular the treatment of the brand and of the expected synergies.
modelAnswer:
Book value of SA's net assets = 180 + 110 = 290. Identifiable intangible: the brand is separable and measurable → recognised at fair value 120. Expected synergies are not an identifiable asset – they are part of goodwill.
Goodwill = price 950 − (290 + 120) = 540.
Consolidated balance sheet: Equipment 520 + 380 = 900 · Cash 950 − 950 = 0 · Brand 120 · Goodwill 540 → total 1,560.
Capital 700 · Net income 60 (only PC's; SA's equity at acquisition is eliminated against the investment) · Liabilities 710 + 90 = 800 → total 1,560.

steps.title: Book value of SA's net assets
Identifiable intangibles
steps.why: IFRS 3: an intangible is recognised if it is separable or arises from contractual/legal rights and can be measured. The brand qualifies → 120. Expected synergies are not an identifiable asset → they are part of goodwill.

pitfalls: Recognising the synergies (70) as a separate asset.
Forgetting that PC's cash goes to 0 after paying 950.

topic: PPE – initial cost of a building
prompt: At what amount should the building be recognised on 1 January 2025? Justify which items you include.
modelAnswer:
Cost of a self-constructed asset = all costs directly attributable to bringing it to working condition: raw materials 600,000 + salaries of construction workers 2,200,000 + depreciation of equipment used 150,000 = 2,950,000.
Excluded: the land (3,000,000) is a separate asset that is not depreciated; the opening party (90,000) and the moving costs (40,000) are not needed to bring the building to working condition and are expensed.
keyPoints: Opening party and moving costs expensed

steps.title: Principle (IAS 16)
steps.why: Cost of a self-constructed asset = all costs directly attributable to bringing it to working condition.

steps.title: Exclude
lines: Opening party 90,000 → not necessary for the asset → expense
Moving staff in 40,000 → after the asset is ready → expense

pitfalls: Capitalising the opening party – like the party after installing a machine (mock questions), it is an expense.

prompt: What are the balance sheet and income statement impacts on 31 December 2025?
modelAnswer: Under the cost model the fair value (3,000,000) is not used. Depreciation 2025 = 2,950,000 / 25 = 118,000 → expense in the income statement; the carrying amount falls to 2,950,000 − 118,000 = 2,832,000. (The fair value is above the carrying amount, so there is no indication of impairment.)
keyPoints: Fair value ignored under the cost model

steps.title: Cost model
steps.why: The fair value (3,000,000) is ignored – no revaluation.

prompt: On 1 January 2027 Toledo spends €250,000 on modifications that extend the building's useful life by 5 years. What are the accounting impacts in 2027, and what is the carrying amount on 31 December 2027?
modelAnswer:
Carrying amount end of 2026 = 2,950,000 − 2 × 118,000 = 2,714,000.
The modifications extend the useful life, so they are capitalised: 2,714,000 + 250,000 = 2,964,000 on 1 January 2027.
Remaining useful life = 25 − 2 + 5 = 28 years (change in estimate, applied prospectively).
Depreciation 2027 = 2,964,000 / 28 = 105,857.14 (expense).
Carrying amount 31 December 2027 = 2,964,000 − 105,857.14 = 2,858,142.86.

steps.title: Capitalise the modification
steps.why: Subsequent expenditure that extends the useful life (future economic benefits) is added to the asset.

steps.title: New remaining useful life (change in estimate, prospective)

pitfalls: Expensing the 250,000 – it extends the useful life, so it is capitalised.
Restating 2025–2026 depreciation (changes in estimates are prospective).

prompt: Describe briefly the problems you may encounter as a reader of financial statements when you try to compare non-GAAP KPIs, such as free cash flow, published by two different companies.
modelAnswer: Non-GAAP KPIs are not defined by IFRS, so each company chooses its own definition: Which definition did each company use (e.g. FCF before or after interest, leases, acquisitions, dividends to NCI)? Are the numbers reconciled to IFRS figures (cash flow statement, income statement) so I can recompute them? Are definitions stable over time, or changed when a different definition looks better? Are they audited? Is management selective in what it adjusts (e.g. excluding “one-off” costs every year)? Only after harmonising the definitions can the KPIs be compared.

steps.title: Root cause
steps.why: Non-GAAP KPIs are not defined by IFRS – each company chooses its own definition.

steps.title: Questions a reader must ask
lines: Which definition? (FCF before/after interest, leases, acquisitions, dividends to NCI)
Is there a reconciliation to IFRS figures so I can recompute it?
Has the definition changed over time?

options.text: that are confidential but audited by the company's auditors
that are not defined by any accounting standard
whose disclosure is mandatory under IFRS
whose disclosure is mandatory under stock-exchange rules for listed companies

explanation: Non-GAAP (alternative performance) measures such as EBITDA or free cash flow are defined by the company itself, not by IFRS. They are published voluntarily, are usually not audited, and regulators only require that they are explained and reconciled.

prompt: Earnings per share (EPS) according to IFRS …

options.text: is net income attributable to the ordinary shareholders of the parent divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding
is a non-GAAP KPI that many companies publish voluntarily
is the dividend a shareholder receives per share
is net income attributable to all ordinary shareholders (parent and subsidiaries) divided by the weighted average number of all ordinary shares outstanding

explanation: IAS 33 defines EPS: profit attributable to the parent's ordinary shareholders (i.e. after NCI) divided by the weighted average number of the parent's ordinary shares outstanding. It is an IFRS measure, not non-GAAP, and has nothing to do with dividends.

prompt: On 1 January 2025, Finchley Ltd leases an office building for 20 years. The present value of the lease payments, discounted at 5%, is €3,000,000 (rounded). Lease payments of €240,000 are due on 31 December each year, the first on 31 December 2025. The right-of-use asset is depreciated straight-line over the lease term. What is the impact on the financial statements for 2025 under IFRS 16?

options.text: Rent expense and cash outflow of €240,000
Right-of-use asset €3,000,000, lease liability €3,000,000, depreciation €150,000, rent expense and cash outflow €240,000
Right-of-use asset €2,850,000, lease liability €2,910,000, interest expense €150,000, depreciation €150,000, cash outflow €240,000
Right-of-use asset €2,850,000, lease liability €3,000,000, depreciation €150,000, rent expense and cash outflow €240,000
Right-of-use asset €2,850,000, lease liability €2,760,000, depreciation €150,000, interest expense €0, cash outflow €240,000

explanation: At commencement: right-of-use asset = lease liability = 3,000,000. 2025: depreciation 3,000,000 / 20 = 150,000 → ROU 2,850,000. Interest 5% × 3,000,000 = 150,000; the payment of 240,000 covers the interest and repays 90,000 → liability 2,910,000. There is no rent expense under IFRS 16.

prompt: Under IFRS 16, for which contracts must Halden recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability if it applies the optional exemptions?

options.text: Only contract A, because only its term covers the whole economic life of the asset
Contracts A and B
Contracts A, B and C
All four contracts
None – IFRS 16 only requires disclosure in the notes

explanation: IFRS 16 has no operating/finance distinction for lessees: every lease goes on the balance sheet, also contract B although it covers only half the van's life. Exemptions: contract C is a short-term lease (≤ 12 months) and contract D a lease of low-value assets (laptops) – their payments may be expensed straight-line.

prompt: Calculate the lease liability that Halden recognises at commencement for contracts A and B.
modelAnswer:
Lease liability = present value of the lease payments at 10%.
Contract A: 100,000 × 4.3553 = 435,530.
Contract B: 20,000 × 2.4869 = 49,738.
The right-of-use assets are recognised at the same amounts (no initial direct costs or prepayments).

steps.title: Rule
steps.why: Lease liability = PV of the lease payments not yet paid, discounted at the implicit rate or the incremental borrowing rate (10%).

steps.title: Contract B
steps.result: A 435,530; B 49,738 (ROU assets at the same amounts)

steps.title: Why not C and D?
steps.why: C (10 months) is a short-term lease and D (laptops ≈ €900 each) a low-value lease → exemption, payments expensed.

prompt: Which statement about the lessee's accounting under IFRS 16 is CORRECT?

options.text: At commencement, the lessee generally expenses each lease payment in the period it is paid.
At commencement, the lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability measured at the present value of the lease payments.
The leased asset is shown in the balance sheet at its fair value and revalued every year.
Only leases that transfer ownership at the end of the term are recognised in the balance sheet.
The lessee recognises a receivable equal to the net investment in the lease.

explanation: IFRS 16 uses a single lessee model: right-of-use asset and lease liability at the PV of the lease payments; afterwards depreciation and interest. Expensing payments (a) was the old IAS 17 operating-lease treatment; a receivable (e) is the lessor's side of a finance lease.
